analysis.one_liner: Caps economy-wide global warming pollution through cap-and-trade, plus clean electricity and vehicle standards.
analysis.headline: An ambitious 2007 Senate bill to cap economy-wide carbon emissions never got past the Finance Committee — no vote, no markup, no action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set up a nationwide cap-and-trade system requiring the biggest emitters of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases to hold allowances for each ton they emit, with the number of allowances shrinking until emissions are 65% below 2000 levels by 2050. It would have auctioned the allowances — forbidding free giveaways that create windfall profits — and spent the proceeds through a Climate Reinvestment Fund. It also would have required cleaner passenger vehicles, rising shares of renewable electricity, and consumer tax credits for efficient cars.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who bear the costs of climate change and air pollution — coastal communities, farmers, and anyone exposed to extreme weather — along with consumers who could claim tax credits for efficient vehicles. The bill specifically directed implementers to soften energy cost increases for low-income consumers and to help workers and regions dependent on coal.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, workers, and communities facing climate risk

how_it_helps.text: Sets binding targets to cut U.S. global warming pollution to 1990 levels by 2020 and 65% below 2000 levels by 2050, aimed at keeping warming below 2 degrees Celsius.

Requires allowances to be auctioned and bars any free distribution that would create windfall profits for polluters, with auction proceeds and fines flowing into a Climate Reinvestment Fund to pursue the bill's goals.

Doubles existing tax credits for fuel cell and efficient hybrid vehicles, creates a new plug-in hybrid credit worth up to about $6,000, and gives automakers a 35% credit for retooling factories to build advanced vehicles.

Requires passenger vehicle emission standards at least as strict as California's 2004 rules, a renewable electricity requirement rising to 20% by 2021, and annual utility energy-savings targets backed by a 4-cents-per-kilowatt-hour fee for noncompliance.

Requires large public companies to tell investors about their climate-related financial risks, and directs help for low-income consumers and transition assistance for workers and regions shifting away from high-carbon energy.

analysis.who_pays: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers and energy-intensive manufacturers, who would need to buy allowances or cut emissions; electric utilities facing renewable and efficiency mandates; major oil companies, which would have to install E-85 pumps at up to half their stations at their own expense. Some energy costs would pass through to consumers, though the bill directs implementers to cushion low-income households.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy-intensive industry

drawbacks.text: A cap-and-trade system raises energy prices before clean alternatives fully scale, and those costs fall hardest on households in coal-dependent regions — a cost its supporters would have to acknowledge, even with the bill's low-income protections.

Creating a nationwide market in emission allowances builds a large new financial market subject to price swings, speculation, and lobbying over allowance rules, and the auction revenue would be spent at the President's discretion without further congressional appropriation.

The biofuel provisions lock in huge ethanol volumes — at least 60 billion gallons by 2030 — and require oil companies to install E-85 pumps regardless of ethanol's actual climate benefit, steering public policy toward the farm-based fuel industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core — a declining cap with auctioned allowances and explicit bans on polluter windfalls — was a more aggressive design than later cap-and-trade proposals, and it paired emission limits with real consumer credits and transition aid. Its weaknesses are the inherent cost pass-through of any carbon cap and the generous carve-outs for ethanol. On balance it was a serious attempt to address a problem whose costs fall on ordinary people, paid for mainly by concentrated fossil fuel interests.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2007 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it before that Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. John Kerry introduced the bill on February 1, 2007, joined by Republican Sen. Olympia Snowe, making it a bipartisan introduction.

The Senate's only action was to read it twice and refer it to the Committee on Finance; the action history records no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 110th Congress.
Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died in committee with only two cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and electric utilities were better off: they faced no federal emissions cap during the 110th Congress because the committee never acted. Consumers and communities exposed to climate risk lost the chance the bill represented.

against.what_they_did: Opposed economy-wide carbon cap-and-trade legislation during this period, contributing to the climate in which no such bill reached a floor vote in the 110th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; sponsorship was bipartisan (a Democrat lead sponsor and one Republican cosponsor), but with only two cosponsors there is no record of broader party positioning either way.

industries.note: The cap would have required the largest emitters to buy shrinking allowances or cut emissions, with a civil penalty of twice the allowance price for excess emissions. Avoiding any cap spared them those compliance costs, which would otherwise have been borne by shareholders and passed partly to consumers.

Retail electricity suppliers would have faced rising renewable-energy requirements (20% by 2021), annual energy-savings targets, and a 4-cents-per-kilowatt-hour fee for missing them. Compliance costs would reach customers, but the efficiency mandate also cuts customer bills over time.

They would have had to meet passenger-vehicle emission standards at least as strict as California's 2004 rules, but received a new 35% manufacturing investment credit and doubled consumer purchase credits to help sell efficient vehicles.

The bill requires renewable fuel volumes rising to at least 60 billion gallons by 2030 and forces major oil companies to install E-85 pumps at up to half their stations at their own expense, creating guaranteed demand and infrastructure for ethanol regardless of its climate performance.
A national renewable electricity requirement with tradable credits creates a growing market for wind, solar, and other renewable generators, backed by penalties for utilities that do not comply.

The bill makes emission allowances freely tradable and bankable, creating a large new commodities market. It bans free allowances that create windfall profits, but the trading system itself would enrich market intermediaries.
